terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo runs both functions on a short series and times windowMax on a longer one.

tasks.title: Window maximum, any way you like
tasks.description:
Implement `windowMax(nums, k)` in `src/windowMax.ts`. It returns the maximum of every window of `k` consecutive numbers, from left to right: `nums.length - k + 1` values.

- `k` is a whole number of at least 1. When `k` is larger than `nums.length`, return `[]`.
- Do not change `nums`.

This task only uses small inputs, so a direct approach that looks at every window is fine. The check covers `k` of 1, `k` equal to the length, `k` larger than the length, an empty array, negative numbers and repeated values.
nextSteps: Work out how many windows there are and where each one starts.
Compute the maximum of each window and collect them.
Try negative numbers and `k` larger than the array in the demo.
Run `node src/demo.ts` and read the first line.
hints: The windows start at indexes 0 to `nums.length - k`. If that is negative, there are none.
A starting maximum of 0 breaks windows of negative numbers. Start from the first number of the window or from `-Infinity`.
Two nested loops are enough here: the outer one over window starts, the inner one over the `k` numbers of the window.

tasks.title: Window maximum in linear time
tasks.description:
Make `windowMax` run in O(n), whatever `k` is.

The check runs it on a million random, falling and rising numbers with windows of 1,000 to 50,000, compares the results with a correct answer and expects each run to finish in under 1 second. Looking at every number of a window again is too slow, even if you only do it when the maximum leaves the window: falling numbers make that happen on every step.

A couple of small cases with repeated values check that numbers leave the window by position, not by value.
nextSteps: Read the monotonic deque section of the lesson.
Keep indexes, not values, in your deque.
On each step: drop smaller candidates from the back, add the new index, drop the front if it left the window.
Run the demo and compare the time on the last line with task 1.
hints: A number that has a larger number after it inside the window can never be a window maximum again. You can forget it.
If you only keep numbers that are not followed by a larger one, they are in decreasing order, and the first one is the maximum.
`Array.prototype.shift` is O(n). Use a head index into an array instead, so removing from the front is O(1).

tasks.title: Longest stretch within a limit
tasks.description:
Implement `longestWithin(nums, limit)` in `src/longestWithin.ts`. It returns the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers whose maximum minus minimum is at most `limit`.

- `limit` is at least 0. An empty array gives 0. A single number is a run of length 1.
- Do not change `nums`.

The check covers limit 0, a run covering the whole array, negative numbers and a run that must shrink from its start. It also runs a million slowly wandering numbers, where the best run is thousands long, and expects it to finish in under 1 second.
nextSteps: Use a window with a start and an end that both only move right.
Keep one deque for the maximum and one for the minimum of the window.
When the window gets too wide, move its start right and drop deque fronts that fell out.
Record the best length after each step and run the demo.
hints: This is a window whose size changes. The end moves one step per number; the start moves only when the window breaks the limit.
The maximum deque is the one from task 2. The minimum deque is the same with the comparison flipped.
After adding index `i` to both deques, while `max - min > limit`, move `start` forward and drop a deque front whose index is now below `start`. Then the window `start..i` qualifies.
